This message comes from Angie. Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled
pros to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs
to major remodels, find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder. President Trump rallied Republican voters in Ohio
Wednesday. Former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in Georgia,
both making last-ditch efforts to attract votes ahead of midterm election day.
Millions have already voted, Democrats leading the early vote, but NPR's Domenico
Montanaro warns against reading too much into that.
Early voting is pretty robust. We're six days out and almost 40 million people have voted,
and that's climbing, but it would be folly to read too much into early voting.
Republicans overwhelmingly vote on election day in person, so that's a big wild card here.
In the states that do report early votes by party, so far the split is 44% Democratic to 31%
Republican. That may sound like a big Democratic advantage, but even in a year when they lost
seats in the House like 2022, Democrats won early voting 43 to 44. So not a huge difference from
then to now. In Alaska's tight U.S. Senate race, Democrat Mary Peltola did not directly refute a
New York Times report that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan Sullivan to join the
race, to give her an advantage as she tries to unseat the incumbent Republican who is also named
Dan Sullivan. Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin reports. Republicans have alleged for months that
the second Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to draw votes away from the Senator. The Times
story seems to substantiate that claim, although NPR has not independently confirmed that reporting.
Peltola dismissed the story as a distraction. Nobody at the New York Times cares about
affordability in Alaska. Super PACs often promote spoilers in Alaska elections. The state's rank
choice voting method is intended to blunt the spoiler effect, but not all voters rank their
ballots. For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage. King Charles and Queen Camilla on a nine-day tour
of former British colonies in the Caribbean, protesters have gathered at some of the King's
events demanding reparations for slavery during the British Empire. NPR's Lauren Freya reports
from London. At a youth rally in the Bahamas, King Charles said the country's culture was born out of
darkness. It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past.
But the monarch stopped short of apologizing for how his royal ancestors presided over and
profited from shipping millions of enslaved Africans to the Caribbean. The issue of reparations
is expected to come up at a Commonwealth summit starting Sunday in Antigua, which the King is
attending. The secretary general of that group of mostly former British colonies has said the quote
"time has come for a discussion about compensation." The royals have previously expressed sorrow for
the past but ruled out reparations. Lauren Freya and PR News London. This is NPR.
Spain has begun three days of national mourning following Wednesday's deadly train collision.
At least 68 people were killed and dozens were injured when a high-speed train collided with
another train in the central province of Toledo. Rescue workers searched through the records through
the night and protesters in Madrid were on the streets demanding government accountability.
Labor rights activist Dolores Huerta died Wednesday at the age of 96 at her home
in Bakersfield, California. She was instrumental in improving rights for farm workers and women.
Omaré Alvarez of member station KVPR revisited a mural of the late activist in downtown Bakersfield.
The mural features Huerta shouting into a rainbow-colored megaphone. Flowers and candles
were placed in front of it. Huerta is remembered for her famous protest chant "si se puede,
yes we can." Manpreet Khar is the vice mayor of Bakersfield. She says Huerta paved the way
for women of color. As an elected official, a woman in public office, it feels a little bit
lonelier knowing that Dolores isn't there to pull us up onto the stage and say yes you can.
Earlier this year, Huerta publicly accused late civil rights leader Cesar Chavez of sexual
assault. Other women have come forward with allegations. For NPR News, I'm Amre Alvarez
in Bakersfield. Major League Baseball has a first-time champion. The Milwaukee Brewers won
the best of seven World Series and five games Wednesday night, beating the Tampa Bay Rays
4-1. I'm Giles Snyder. This is NPR News. This message comes from NetSuite. AI is changing the

Former President Obama campaigns for Democrats in Georgia ahead of midterms

Alaska Senate race: Peltola's team reportedly recruited a same-named Dan Sullivan as spoiler
King Charles and Queen Camilla tour Caribbean amid protests demanding slavery reparations
King Charles calls Bahamian culture born of darkness but stops short of apology
Commonwealth summit in Antigua expected to discuss reparations and compensation
Spain declares three days of national mourning after deadly high-speed train collision in Toledo
